threats.name: Use After Free
threats.rationale: OCaml's garbage collector frees memory only when it is unreachable, so a managed OCaml program cannot hold a dangling reference. The ways out of that guarantee are Obj.* tricks, `external` C stubs, unsafe accessors and Bigarray unsafe reads. The library is list-only code (no Array, Bytes, String or Bigarray, by reading) and the merged analyzer hard-bans Obj.* and Marshal.from_* and flags `external` (effectively banned while required_capabilities is empty) (ocaml.merged-banned-constructs). The remaining half of the exclusion, a ban on the unsafe accessors, does not exist yet.

threats.name: Integer Overflow to Buffer Boundary

The widths are capped or tied to list lengths today only for decoder. Integer wraparound in general is the separate lane threat ocaml.integer-wraparound-and-shift; this row must never be rendered as 'integer overflow excluded'.

threats.name: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption
threats.rationale: Real finding. Resource use is driven by caller-supplied sizes. decoder is capped at 16 bits (ml:75, :132, tested at test:98-100), but demux builds List.init n_outputs (ml:126) for any power-of-two n_outputs once the caller supplies log2(n_outputs) selector bits, shift_register and counter build List.init width (ml:302, :347-348) for any positive ?width, and nothing bounds the list inputs of mux_n, encoder or the n-ary gates (linear in a length the caller already paid for). The registry has no route for a list-returning package: pure_zero_allocation is false (boxed Ok values and lists), and the discharge needs a microbenchmark-zero-alloc item that cannot be true for an API that returns lists, a step-bound proof (no OCaml proof tool) and an input-bounds check. The lane does not map the registry id microbenchmark-zero-alloc to an allocation-bound benchmark: that would redefine it. The caps, the allocation benchmark and the step-bound rule stay as closure items (planned) but no route claims they satisfy the registry ids, so the class cannot close here (python and typescript precedent).

closed_by.detail: Caps and their bound tests: a documented ceiling on demux n_outputs and on the width of register, shift_register and counter (the cap on mux_n/encoder/n-ary input list lengths is in LGE-OCAML-HARDEN), each returning Invalid_width or Invalid_length before any allocation, with a test at the cap and at cap+1. Today only decoder is capped (ml:75, :132; test :98-100); README.md:8-12 documents only that cap.

Every loop or List operation is bounded by a caller list length or by a capped width, does constant work per element, and no allocation size depends on an uncapped int. Run today it would flag ml:126 (List.init n_outputs in demux), :302 (List.init width in shift_register) and :347-348 (List.init width in counter).

A BUILD-run microbenchmark of Gc.minor_words and Gc.allocated_bytes per call for every gate at the cap and at cap+1. threats.rationale: OCaml native ints on the 64-bit target CI uses are 63 bits wide and wrap silently modulo 2^63 (32-bit bytecode and js_of_ocaml differ and are not covered); `lsl` by a negative amount or by Sys.int_size or more has an unspecified result. The library shifts in index_of_selectors (ml:77-82, `bit lsl shift`, shift = position in a caller selector list), computes `1 lsl width` for decoder (:136, width capped at 16 at :75/:132) and `lsr` in bits_of_index (:139-140). By reading every shift is in range: mux and demux compare the selector length with log2 of the input count before indexing (:97-100, :118-122), and the count is at most 2^61 for a power of two that fits a positive int. That argument depends on the validations holding, and the demux case is a 61-bit selector list shifting up to bit 60. The value-range rule is the same idea as the C lane's c.integer-value-range.

closed_by.detail: A value-range dataflow, not a syntactic rule: each +, -, lsl, lsr and land is shown, from the validated operand ranges (a bit is 0 or 1 after valid_bit, a selector list length is at most the cap) never to wrap past 2^62-1 and never to shift by a negative or >= Sys.int_size amount. Sites today: ml:26, :28-29, :38, :47-49, :78-82, :136, :139-140, :330-331.

threats.name: Numeric Truncation Error (caller-side)
threats.rationale: Gates take OCaml `int`. A caller holding an Int64, Int32, nativeint, float or char must convert explicitly, and `Int64.to_int` takes its argument modulo 2^63 (so the Int64 value 2^63 + 1 becomes 1, a valid bit), `Int32.to_int` is lossless but `Int32.of_int` truncates, and `int_of_float` truncates toward zero (so 1.9 becomes 1). The library cannot see the caller's wider value: it only receives the already-narrowed int and accepts it if it is 0 or 1. This is the one OCaml row the package cannot close; every release must say so.

Escape hatches (Obj, Marshal.from_*, external) are covered by analyzer-rule:ocaml.merged-banned-constructs.

threats.name: Incorrect Comparison (polymorphic compare)
threats.rationale: OCaml's `=`, `<>` and `compare` are polymorphic: on ints they are specialised and exact, on lists they recurse structurally, on functional values they raise, on cyclic values they loop and on floats `=` treats nan as unequal to itself. The library uses them on ints (valid_bit at ml:16, the length checks) and once on two int lists (ml:370), all correct today; the hazard is a future edit that compares a richer type, or a float that sneaked in through a conversion. A typed rule can require monomorphic comparison (Int.equal, List.equal Int.equal).

threats.name: Operator Precedence Logic Error
threats.rationale: A gate is operators: `land`, `lor`, `lxor`, `lsl`, `1 - x`. The merged truth tables compute their expectations with the same operators (test:23-28), so they cannot catch a mis-parse; PR #19949 replaces them with literal tables.

considered_not_included.why_not: Folded into ocaml.build-dependency-trust (opam archive checksums, --require-checksums); the package downloads nothing at run time.

considered_not_included.name: Use of Potentially Dangerous Function
considered_not_included.why_not: Folded into the Obj, unsafe-accessor and partial-function rules (ocaml.unsafe-accessors-and-compiler-flags, ocaml.partial-functions-and-uncaught-exceptions).

considered_not_included.why_not: Folded into CWE-704 (package side) and ocaml.caller-side-int-narrowing (caller side).

considered_not_included.name: Improper Handling of Exceptional Conditions
considered_not_included.why_not: The Lazy.force case (a thunk that raises re-raises on every force, and a recursive force raises Lazy.Undefined) does not arise: the library has no lazy value (no match in ml:1-385). The general exception case is ocaml.partial-functions-and-uncaught-exceptions.

considered_not_included.name: Reliance on Undefined, Unspecified, or Implementation-Defined Behavior
considered_not_included.why_not: OCaml leaves argument evaluation order unspecified and `lsl` out of range unspecified; the library's operations are pure so evaluation order is not observable, and the shift case is ocaml.integer-wraparound-and-shift.

considered_not_included.name: Missing Release of Resource after Effective Lifetime
considered_not_included.why_not: The library opens no channel or handle (no filesystem rule fires, required_capabilities.json:5 is empty).

considered_not_included.name: Access of Uninitialized Pointer
considered_not_included.why_not: OCaml has no pointers and no uninitialised values.

considered_not_included.name: Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere
considered_not_included.why_not: Folded into ocaml.build-dependency-trust: the library includes no third-party module; dune plugins and ppx are build-time.

considered_not_included.name: Deadlock

considered_not_included.why_not: Folded into CWE-94 (Dynlink, Toploop) and CWE-843 (Obj).
